analysis.one_liner: Shuts down EPA grant programs, climate work, regional offices, and ozone and greenhouse-gas rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: with no cosponsors, it sat in four House committees until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended every EPA grant program, barred the EPA from creating new ones, and cut off funding for enforcing new ozone air-quality standards, regulating greenhouse gases from cars and power plants, tracking emissions, running climate resilience programs, and doing climate research. It would also have closed the EPA's regional and field offices and ended its environmental justice programs. It never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in any committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main winners would be fossil fuel producers and coal- and gas-fired power plants, which would face no EPA greenhouse-gas rules for cars, planes, or power plants, no emissions reporting, and no methane initiative. Polluting facilities would also benefit from the ban on implementing any new ozone air-quality standard and from the closure of EPA field offices that do local inspections and enforcement support.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fossil fuel producers and polluting facilities

how_it_helps.text: The bill terminates every EPA grant program then in effect and bars the agency from creating new ones [S2][S3].
It prohibits the EPA from spending any federal money to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from cars, trains, planes, and other mobile sources, or from fossil fuel-fired power plants [S2][S3].

It blocks funding for implementing any ozone air-quality standard issued after enactment, as well as the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, the Global Methane Initiative, climate resilience funds and tools, green infrastructure, climate-ready water utility programs, and climate research at the EPA's Office of Research and Development [S2][S3].
It terminates the National Clean Diesel Campaign and the EPA's environmental justice programs, and requires the agency to discontinue its regional, state, district, and local field offices [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost through weaker air quality protections, especially from the ban on new ozone standards, and through the loss of EPA grants that state and local governments, tribes, and communities use for water quality, clean diesel fleets, air monitoring, and local environmental cleanup. Communities with high pollution exposure would lose the agency's environmental justice programs outright, and the closure of field offices would thin the federal presence that supports local enforcement.
analysis.who_pays_short: State and local governments and polluted communities

drawbacks.text: Terminating all EPA grants would cut off funding that states, tribes, and local governments rely on for water infrastructure, air monitoring, and cleanups — costs that would fall on local taxpayers or simply go unmet [S2][S3].

Barring implementation of any new ozone standard would prevent stronger protections against smog, which medical groups link to asthma and respiratory illness; closing field offices would remove the staff closest to local pollution problems [S2][S3].

Supporters' good-faith case is that some EPA programs duplicate state efforts and that the agency's reach should be narrowed; the counterargument in the bill's own design is that it eliminates everything at once, including reporting and research that even critics of regulation use, and exempts property sales from normal requirements including homeless-assistance conveyance rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a broad, one-time shutdown of most of the EPA's non-enforcement work — grants, climate programs, research, and field offices — with no replacement funding or structure. Its benefits flow to regulated industries, while its costs fall on air quality, climate data, and the state and local programs that grants support. The magnitude of what it would eliminate far exceeds the efficiency gains its supporters could claim.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees and two subcommittees, but no committee ever held a markup or sent it to the floor, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Johnson introduced the bill on February 7, 2017, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, and Science, Space, and Technology Committees [S1][S3][S5].
No member joined as a cosponsor [S4].

The bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment and to the Subcommittee on Environment, but no further action was taken in committee or on the House floor through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, EPA grant programs, climate rules, regional offices, and environmental justice programs continued operating for the rest of the Congress. Fossil fuel interests and regulated polluters gained nothing, while state and local governments kept receiving EPA grants.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA programs kept running; polluters gained nothing

for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill in the House

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded [S4].

industries.industry: Fossil fuel producers and fossil-fired power plants
industries.note: The bill would have barred EPA regulation of their greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles and power plants, ended emissions reporting, and killed the Global Methane Initiative. Their gain comes at the direct cost of climate and air-quality protections for the public.
Blocking any new ozone standard, closing EPA field offices, and terminating grants would weaken the monitoring and local support infrastructure that underpins air and water enforcement.

They receive EPA grants for water quality, air monitoring, clean diesel fleets, and resilience planning; the bill terminates all of them with no replacement, pushing costs onto local budgets and taxpayers.
The bill requires disposal or leasing of EPA property identified as underutilized, exempt from several normal disposal rules, creating disposal work but reducing federal facility activity.
